A data subject complained that the Tax Administration handled their access request badly. They had asked for copies of their data by email or post, with delivery to their agent in Finland, and were told to sign a form, submit it on paper and collect the answer in person. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the handling did not comply with Article 12(2) GDPR, because requiring signed paper forms and in-person or postal submission makes exercising rights unnecessarily difficult. The Tax Administration was ordered to bring its handling of access requests, including the use of agents, into compliance and to process the complainant's 8 April 2020 request. It was also reprimanded for requiring the request to be resubmitted on paper, signed, on a specific form and by post. The question of correcting the phone number was not decided; the controller was given guidance to assess it.

The DPA found that a data subject’s consent to the processing of their health data by an insurance broker was not freely given since the consent was a condition for a discount on a mortgage’s interest rate.

Apoteket AB, a Swedish pharmacy chain, used the Meta pixel on its website with the advanced matching function switched on from January 2020 to April 2022. As a result, hashed contact details, national ID numbers and data on purchases of privacy-sensitive products were sent to Meta. Apoteket reported the incident itself after an outsider alerted it. IMY found that Apoteket had not taken appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 32(1) given the high risks. It rated the infringement as low severity but not minor, and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 37,000,000.

Apohem AB, an online pharmacy, had a Meta pixel on its website with the Automatic Advanced Matching function switched on by mistake. From 15 April 2021 to 26 April 2022 this sent customers' names, contact details, purchase information and IP addresses to Meta, linked to roughly 15,000 people. IMY found that the company had not taken appropriate technical and organisational measures and had no routines to follow up unintended changes in its systems, which breached Article 32(1) GDPR. IMY rated the infringement as low gravity but still imposed an administrative fine of SEK 8,000,000, rejecting a reprimand because the data were privacy-sensitive and the processing carried a high risk.

A customer of a telecommunications company asked for access to his data on 25 January 2022, including who among its employees had accessed it and why. The company asked for clarification, said it could not provide the information, and only gave a satisfactory answer on 28 March 2023, after the Litigation Chamber had opened the case on the merits, about 14 months after the request. The Chamber found a continuing breach of the right of access and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 100,000, treating the breach as of low gravity but caused by serious negligence. A later note says the Market Court partially annulled the decision on 22 January 2025 and reduced the fine to EUR 5,000.
The DPA fined Santander €50,000 for processing a data subject’s personal data for advertisement purposes even after the data subject objected to the respective processing.
The DPA reprimanded a food delivery company for violating Article 44 GDPR by transferring personal data of website users to the USA without any appropriate transfer instrument in place.

An employee of a processor working for the bank mistakenly sent clients' bank documents to another bank, and the envelope had been opened when it came back. The bank notified the breach to the regulator but decided not to tell the clients, arguing that the recipient was a trusted party bound by banking secrecy. The UODO President found that this was a breach of Article 34(1) and (2) GDPR, because the recipient was not a 'trusted recipient' under the EDPB guidelines and the risk to the individuals was high. He fined the bank PLN 4,053,173 (about EUR 928,498) and ordered it to notify the affected clients within 7 days. The decision is not yet final.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation of Ana Hotels SRL in July 2024, started after the company notified a personal data breach. A ransomware attack led to unauthorised disclosure of employees' personal data. The authority found the operator had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures under Article 32 GDPR. It fined the company 39,763.20 lei (about EUR 8,000) and ordered a procedural plan for regular testing of IT systems, continuous logging of access and traffic for at least 30 days, and backups.

The Austrian DSB fined the Austrian subsidiary of a retail group EUR 1,500,000 for operating a nine-camera video surveillance system at one store, from 25 March 2022 to at least 23 May 2022. Three cameras covered the checkout and self-service area, including the card terminal keypad, and four covered the outside area. The DSB found breaches of Art. 5(1)(a) and (c) and Art. 6(1) GDPR, treated them as one processing operation under the absorption principle of Art. 83(3), and set the fine under Art. 83(5)(a) using the group's turnover. The Bundesverwaltungsgericht confirmed the fine on 25 July 2025, and a revision to the Verwaltungsgerichtshof is pending.

The DPA held that a website that publishes the salary of public companies' managers rightfully rejected an erasure request, since the publication of this data is necessary for exercising the right of freedom of expression and information.

The Danish DPA reported Vejen Municipality to the police and recommended a fine of DKK 200,000 for inadequate security measures. The case began when the municipality notified a breach after five laptops were stolen. The laptops, used by teachers and pupils, held information about pupils, including pupils with special challenges, and none were encrypted. The investigation showed about 300 other computers in the municipality were also unencrypted. In Denmark fines under the GDPR are decided by the courts; the DPA’s update says the case was settled in the district court (byretten), where the municipality agreed to pay a fine of DKK 200,000.

An employee of Uniqlo's Spanish branch asked for their payslip and received an email with a PDF containing the payslips of 447 workers, including names, ID numbers, social security numbers and bank account numbers. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings for breach of confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f)) and inadequate security (Art. 32), proposing fines of EUR 300,000 and EUR 150,000. The company paid EUR 270,000 on 22 July 2024, using both 20% reductions for voluntary payment and acknowledgement of responsibility, so the proceedings were terminated. The AEPD also ordered the company to report within 3 months the technical and organisational measures adopted to secure employees' data.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation in July 2024 into BEST ELAN ONLINE SRL after a complaint from a person who kept receiving unsolicited commercial messages. The person had asked for deletion of their data, including through the operator's own link, but got no reply and the messages continued. During the investigation the operator did not provide the information the authority requested. The authority found a breach of Article 58(1) GDPR, fined the company RON 4,977.1 (about EUR 1,000), and ordered it to hand over all the requested information and documents.

A DPA issued a decision under Article 66 GDPR, prohibiting Meta from sharing advertisements containing the data subject’s data, including fake-ads, on Facebook and Instagram within Poland for three months.

A DPA issued a decision under Article 66 GDPR, prohibiting Meta from sharing advertisements containing data subject’s data, including the fake-ads, on Facebook and Instagram within Poland for three months.
The DPA fined an energy provider €60,000, after its processor erroneously assigned the data subject to a different company and therefore unlawfully disclosed personal data to that company.

A complaint was lodged by a data protection officer, acting for a company's employees and in his own name, that Y did not answer an access request made on 27 September 2023. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision, not a decision on the merits. It found that Y may have breached Article 15 read with Articles 12(3) and 12(4) GDPR, and ordered Y to comply with the access request within 30 days of notification. No fine was imposed.

The DPA issued a warning to the operator of a video surveillance system for ignoring an access request by a data subject and failing to cooperate with the DPA. Thus, the controller violated Article 12(1), Article 12(3) and Article 31 GDPR.

An employee complained to the APD that his professional mailbox access had been suspended and his password changed without his consent, and that his employer did not answer his request for access logs. The Chamber Contentieuse dismissed the complaint on opportunity grounds, without examining the merits. It found the complaint was ancillary to a wider dispute with a disciplinary procedure under way, and that the complaint was filed only three days after the access request, so the employer had no reasonable time to respond. No infringement was found and no fine was imposed.
The DPA fined a doctor €15,000 for sending election advertisements to patients in violation of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, and transparency of data processing.

The Dutch DPA fined Uber Technologies Inc. and Uber B.V. EUR 290 million. Uber transferred personal data of European drivers (account, licence, location, photo, payment, ID, and in some cases criminal and medical data) to its servers in the United States without appropriate safeguards under Chapter V GDPR. The AP found that Uber B.V. was the exporter and Uber Technologies Inc. the importer, rejecting Uber's view that drivers themselves made the transfer. Uber stopped using standard contractual clauses from August 2021 and only later relied on the successor to the Privacy Shield. The AP held that a fine was both appropriate and necessary and would have imposed the same amount under its 2019 fine policy rules. Uber announced it would object.

A complainant received commercial calls, and the AEPD opened an investigation and asked Vodafone España to confirm whether the calls reached the complainant's lines, which Vodafone operates through its LOWI brand. Vodafone only answered that the calling number belonged to another operator since May 2021, and repeated this when the request was reiterated. The AEPD found this obstructed its investigative powers under Article 58(1) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 200,000 for failing to provide access under Article 83(5)(e). It also ordered Vodafone to supply the requested information within ten working days of the decision becoming final.

A former commercial agent complained that Selectra S.p.A. kept his individual company email account active after his contract ended in February 2021. The company backed up the mailbox for three years with MailStore and had a forensic firm search it, and the emails were used in court proceedings. The Garante found that the company's privacy notice was inadequate and that the processing breached the principles of lawfulness, data minimisation and storage limitation, as well as the remote-monitoring rules. It banned further processing of data extracted with MailStore and imposed a fine of EUR 80,000.

The Italian DPA joined several complaints against an energy and gas supplier. Customers had been signed up for energy contracts they never asked for, through door-to-door agents, with forged signatures. Some complaints also concerned late or inadequate replies to access requests. After an on-site inspection, the Garante found breaches of the processing principles (lawfulness, accuracy, storage limitation, security, accountability), of the rules on processors and security, and of the access-right rules. It fined the company EUR 5,000,000, ordered corrective measures (for example a blocking quality call, controls on agents, and segregation of unreliable data), restricted the processing of certain customer data, and ordered publication of the decision.

A clinic company notified a personal data breach after a midwife emailed a patient couple an IVF consent form that had already been filled in with another couple's name, date and place of birth, ID number and chosen treatment type. The patient returned an empty form and confirmed deletion within about two hours, and the company says no IT system was involved. The Garante found the company had breached the integrity and confidentiality principle, the rules on health data, and the security obligations. It issued a reprimand instead of a fine, citing the isolated, non-intentional, minor character of the breach and the company's cooperation.

The Italian DPA examined three personal data breaches affecting INPS's COVID-19 benefit services in spring 2020: personal data cached in a content delivery network, a misconfigured authorisation system for the Bonus Baby Sitting application, and caching of personal data on INPS web servers. INPS had notified two of the breaches in April 2020. The Garante found infringements of Article 5(1)(a) and (f) and 5(2), and of Articles 12, 25, 32 and 34 GDPR, and issued a reprimand (ammonimento) without a fine, citing the exceptional pandemic context and INPS's prompt remedial action. It also ordered publication of the decision on its website.

The health authority ULSS 6 Euganea reported a ransomware attack by two criminal groups on its information systems, which compromised health data of thousands of people. The Garante carried out an inspection and found that no multi-factor authentication was in place for VPN access to the network at the time of the breach. It declared the processing unlawful for breaching the integrity and confidentiality principle and the security obligation. It fined the authority EUR 22,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

Two Norwegian nationals complained, via the Norwegian authority, that a car rental company, Avis Budget Italia, had wrongly linked their personal data to another car's plate, so that their details were passed to Italian police and a motorway toll operator for traffic and toll offences they did not commit. The Garante, as lead authority, found that this was a personal data breach caused by an occasional human data-entry error, with low risk to the two individuals. It closed the case without corrective or sanctioning measures and invited the company to keep checking its technical and organisational measures and staff training.

A patient, through her lawyers, asked the doctor for copies of photographs taken before and after her surgery under GDPR Article 15, and got no reply. The Garante asked the doctor for information about the non-reply and his retention practices, and asked again through the Guardia di Finanza. He did not respond to either request. The Garante found the doctor had breached Article 157 of the Italian Data Protection Code (failure to provide information requested by the authority), sanctionable under Article 166(2), and imposed a EUR 4,000 fine, ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website, and ordered payment within 30 days.

A real estate and condominium management company dismissed an employee in October 2020 but kept his named professional email account active until at least March 2021. It also did not reply to his erasure request of 11 November 2020. The Litigation Chamber found breaches of the purpose limitation, minimisation and storage limitation principles (Art. 5(1)(b), (c), (e)), of the lawfulness rule (Art. 6(1)), and of Articles 12(4) and 17(1). It issued a reprimand and ordered the company to provide a policy on closing mailboxes of departing staff within one month.

A person acting for their minor child complained about video surveillance in a classroom during lessons run by a private company providing education services, and about not being given access to the data. The company relied on legitimate interests (Article 6(1)(f)) for security, staff and visitor protection and incident investigation. The Inspectorate found that the interests did not override the pupils' privacy, that the footage was also used to check the quality of an employee's work, and that the processing was unlawful under Article 5(1)(a). It ordered the video surveillance to stop, the recordings to be destroyed, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000.

In August 2023 the foundation Pere Sihtkapital SA began an online survey of childless women aged 20-44 across Estonia. The Inspectorate issued at least one precept (order) about the survey and then opened misdemeanour proceedings. In those proceedings it fined the foundation EUR 30,000, and the foundation has appealed the decision. The news item stresses that data protection requirements must be checked before processing starts, and that partial compliance is not enough. It states no articles and gives no reasoning.

The DPA fined a controller €180,000 because it lacked a legal basis to transfer data concerning a contested debt to a central solvency register and failed to erase the debt from the data subject's financial records.

The DPA fined a race organiser €15,000 for unlawfully collecting participants' health data related to COVID-19. The organiser failed properly inform the participants and to collect their explicit consent under Article 9(1)(a) GDPR

The Polish DPA was handling a complaint about CCTV monitoring by a sole trader and twice asked the trader for explanations, but received no reply. It then opened separate proceedings of its own motion on the failure to cooperate. The trader also ignored the notice of those proceedings and the request for financial data. The President of UODO found breaches of Articles 31 and 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR and imposed a fine of PLN 21,827, equal to EUR 5,000. The breach was treated as intentional and no mitigating factors were found.

The DPA fined Glovo (a food delivery company) €15,000 after it failed to act on an access request. The DPA considered the fact irrelevant that the request was not sent to the DPO email address but to a different contact point of the controller.
The DPA fined a fintech company €72,000 after its inadequate measures to verify its customer’s identity enabled fraudsters to take out a loan in the name of an unaware data subject.
The DPA fined a controller €4,000 after it shared the data subject’s name on its Google profile. In addition, it did not provide the data subject with the information set by Article 14 GDPR.

The DPA fined a plastic surgery clinic €10,000 after it unlawfully shared before and after pictures of a data subject on its social media account. The DPA highlighted that the pictures contained health data under Article 9(1) GDPR.

A complainant reported that files with personal data of citizens of the Municipality of Alimos could be accessed by anyone online by changing a number in a URL. The flaw came from a faulty software upgrade by the municipality's processor, and about 900 data subjects were affected, including identity cards and passports. The Authority found breaches of security of processing, of the processor contract requirements, and of the breach notification and communication duties. It fined the municipality EUR 10,000 and EUR 5,000, reprimanded it for Article 25(1), and fined the processor EUR 5,000.

A data protection complaint was lodged against the Austrian Court of Auditors, which had published on its website a party donation of about EUR 3,000 made by the complainant, with his name, postcode, date, amount and the recipient party. The authority found that the publication was required by section 6(2) and (3) of the Political Parties Act, which is a legal basis under Article 9(2)(g) GDPR, and that it was proportionate, though it intrudes fairly intensively on the right to secrecy. The complaint was dismissed. The decision is not final: an appeal (Bescheidbeschwerde) was lodged with the Federal Administrative Court.

Postel S.p.A. told the Garante of a ransomware attack by the Medusa group. The attackers stole files containing personal data and published them on the dark web, some data could not be restored, and about 25,000 people were affected. The attacker used two known vulnerabilities that Postel had not patched for almost twelve months. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 25, 32 and 33 GDPR, the last because the breach notification lacked essential elements. It dropped a separate charge that, as a service provider, Postel had not helped its client companies enough after the breach (Article 28(3)(f)). It ordered Postel to carry out vulnerability checks, set up a formal vulnerability management procedure and set target times for spotting and fixing security flaws, and imposed a fine of EUR 900,000.

A parent complained that a teacher at a Treviso state school sent an email through the electronic register to the parents of a student's classmates. The email attached an anonymised health authority order that disclosed a student's Covid-19 positivity. The Garante found this was an unlawful communication of health data without a valid legal basis. It issued a reprimand rather than a fine, citing the school's small size, the single affected person, the isolated nature of the event, the school's full cooperation and the corrective steps it took.

A complainant asked the municipality of Villasimius to erase, and de-index from search engines, a selection-commission minutes document that contained her date of birth, degree grade and evaluations, and the names of the commission members. The municipality only acted after the Garante invited it to respond in September 2022, and the document had been published online until then. The Garante found breaches of Article 12 (late reply to a data subject request), Article 5(1)(a) and Article 6 GDPR, together with the national Article 2-ter of the Codice, and imposed a total fine of EUR 4,000 (EUR 1,000 for the late reply and EUR 3,000 for the unlawful publication). It also ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA opened an investigation after a press article reported that the municipality of Treviso used thermal-camera drones and a citizen reporting app called TrevisoSicura. It found the app processing unlawful: no valid legal basis, inadequate privacy notice, no data processing agreement with the app supplier, and failure to apply data protection by design/default and accountability. It fined the municipality EUR 7,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The complaint about the drones was closed without sanction.

The Veneto regional ombudsman told the Garante that a Vicenza court judgment, with the names of minors not anonymised, was reachable through a link in a commentary article on the Moltocomuni website. The judgment concerned a dispute between two municipalities over the costs of care for minors, and it also showed their residence, the facilities that hosted them and the periods of stay. The publisher removed the article and the judgment and said the omission was an unintentional error. The Garante found a breach of the lawfulness, fairness and minimisation principles and of the Code's rules on publishing judgments and on journalism. It banned further processing other than storage and fined the company EUR 10,000.

After a complaint about weak authentication and default passwords in golf systems, the Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman examined the Finnish Golf Union's eBirdie system. The eBirdie app used membership details instead of passwords as login, which the decision found made unauthorised access to other people's personal data easy. The Ombudsman found breaches of Articles 25(1) and 32(1)(b) GDPR. No fine was imposed: the union received a reprimand and an order to bring its processing into compliance, with a report on measures due by 30 September 2024.

The Lithuanian authority, as lead authority in a cross-border case, fined Vinted, UAB €2,385,276 after complaints forwarded from France and Poland. Vinted rejected or mishandled erasure requests with generic replies that gave only the blocking reason and did not state all grounds for refusal, and it did so while providing incomplete information. The authority also found that the 'shadow blocking' of users' accounts lacked a lawful basis under Art. 6(1)(f) and was not transparent under Art. 13(1)(c). It also found an accountability failure under Art. 5(2). The decision has been appealed to the Regional Administrative Court.

The DPA fined Aldi HUF 80,000,000 (€204,000) in connection to its age verification practices when selling alcohol. It found that data subjects could not easily access information and that they could not be asked for an ID when there was no doubt they were over 18.

Datatilsynet examined, on its own initiative, IDA Forsikring's use of AI speech-to-text analysis of recorded customer-service calls. It found that the company may record and analyse calls within the GDPR, and that the legitimate-interest basis for employee data is acceptable. However, the single consent collected for both documentation and training purposes was not granular, so it was not freely given and could not serve as a legal basis. Datatilsynet issued no criticism, because the question of telephone consent had not been addressed before, but required IDA Forsikring to bring its consent process into compliance going forward.

AXA Real Estate Investment Managers Iberica notified the AEPD of a personal data breach: an encrypted USB device sent by courier (SEUR) was lost, and its access key was in the same envelope. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings for an alleged breach of Article 32 GDPR and proposed a fine of EUR 100,000. The company paid EUR 80,000, taking the 20% reduction for voluntary payment. It did not take the reduction for admitting responsibility. Under Article 85 LPACAP the payment ended the proceedings. The AEPD still ordered the parties to notify it within two months of the security measures described in the initiation agreement.

The Romanian DPA (ANSPDCP) concluded an investigation into Rețele Electrice Muntenia SA following complaints that users logged into their accounts on the shared website www.e.distributie.com could view personal data of other customers. The investigation confirmed that the controller failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure system confidentiality, leading to unauthorized third-party access to customer personal data including names, addresses, and national identification numbers (CNP). Consequently, the authority found infringements of Article 32(1)(b), (d) and Article 32(2) GDPR. ANSPDCP imposed a fine of RON 14,928.60 (approximately EUR 3,000) and ordered the controller to implement periodic security testing for online services on its new customer web portal.

ANSPDCP finished investigations into two electricity distribution operators, Rețele Electrice Muntenia and Rețele Electrice Dobrogea, which share a customer website. A logged-in user of that site could see other customers' personal data. The authority found that the operators had not put in place adequate technical and organisational security measures, so a third party gained unauthorised access to customer data. Rețele Electrice Dobrogea was fined RON 4,976.20 (stated as the equivalent of EUR 1,000) and, like the other operator, ordered to introduce periodic testing of its online services on the new web portal.

A complainant whose bank account was debited by Banco Cetelem for loans of a third party complained to the Spanish AEPD in October 2023. Cetelem had deleted the account data from its database after a first complaint but not from the underlying contract, so further debits occurred in September and October 2023, and it later transferred the debt with the erroneous account number to a third company. The AEPD opened sanctioning proceedings in May 2024 against alleged breaches of Article 6 (twice) and Article 17(1)(d) GDPR. Cetelem paid EUR 150,000 on 31 May 2024 using both the 20% admission reduction and the 20% voluntary payment reduction, and the AEPD declared the procedure terminated and ordered organisational measures.

A data subject complained that a nightclub, Clemens Bar ApS, refused his request for access to CCTV footage showing him. The club argued that disclosure would reveal camera positions and blind spots and that blurring the roughly 150 other people visible was not feasible. Datatilsynet found there was not sufficient basis to set aside the club's refusal under Article 15(4) GDPR. However, the club had deleted the footage after the complaint was lodged, which cut off any review of the refusal, and Datatilsynet issued serious criticism (alvorlig kritik) for breach of the principle of lawfulness, fairness and transparency in Article 5(1)(a).

Avanza Bank notified IMY of a personal data incident: between 15 November 2019 and 2 June 2021 the Meta pixel's Automatic Advanced Matching and Automatic Events functions, activated by mistake, sent data of roughly 500,000 to 1 million people to Meta, including personal identity numbers, loan amounts and account numbers. Much of it was sent in plain text from logged-in areas. IMY found the bank lacked appropriate security measures, did not follow its own routines and could not detect the transfer, breaching Articles 32(1) and 5(1)(f) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 15,000,000, assessing the seriousness as low within the range for Article 5(1)(f) infringements.

A patient complained that a surgeon never answered her access request for the pre-operative photographs taken before her operation. The surgeon only supplied them 302 days later, after the Garante invited him to comply. The Garante also found that the retention period in his privacy notice was too generic. It declared the processing unlawful, fined him EUR 4,000, ordered him to rewrite the notice within 40 days and ordered publication of the decision. The case against the healthcare facility was closed.

A complainant objected that a ranking list from a preselection test of a public competition, naming admitted and non-admitted candidates, stayed online and indexed by search engines on the Municipality of Nepi's website despite removal requests. The Garante found the list was published from 3 February 2015 to 18 February 2022 without a legal basis. It also found the Municipality had no Article 28 data processing agreement with its web management provider until November 2022. It fined the Municipality EUR 8,000 for the publication and EUR 12,000 for the missing processor agreement, EUR 20,000 in total, and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ceased.

A former employee complained that his employer, a food company, had not answered his access request for personal data stored on the company PC he used. The company first refused, citing fear of trade secrets being taken, then said the request was too generic. Access was given only after the Garante opened its investigation, about two years late. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR, fined the company EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian Garante examined two proceedings against telecom operator Fastweb, started after many complaints and reports about unwanted promotional calls, use of customer contact data for marketing, weak information notices and late replies to data subject requests. It found that Fastweb failed to check the Public Opposition Register for numbers called after web-sales consent, relied on legitimate interest instead of consent for marketing to customers (including up to 24 months after contract end), gave unclear privacy notices and did not answer rights requests on time. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000,000 and several corrective orders, including a ban on processing numbers whose marketing consent was collected via websales, a double opt-in system and a rewritten notice and consent form. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA learned from public sources that the municipality of Forlì offered the 'Falco – Città protetta' app, letting citizens send reports to the local police, who could check CCTV images and collect the reporter's GPS position and phone number. After an investigation it found unlawful processing both in the video surveillance systems and in the Falco app, including failures on transparency, privacy by design, processor contract, security and the DPIA. It fined the municipality EUR 10,000 for the video surveillance violations and EUR 5,000 for the Falco violations, EUR 15,000 in total, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ended.

A complainant said the municipality's mayor disclosed her personal data, including traffic fines, to a journalist and at a public event. The Garante found that the Mayor's disclosure of additional details (exact number of fines, penalty points deducted and speed) had no legal basis and breached the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and data minimisation. The Garante issued a reprimand rather than a fine, treating the case as a minor violation because it concerned one data subject, was made in good faith, and the municipality cooperated fully.

A complainant reported that a bus operator had published the personal mobile phone numbers of about 300 bus drivers in a phone directory on its intranet, where all drivers could see them. The operator said it relied on the contract-performance basis in Article 6(1)(b) GDPR and that the phone directory was needed for operational contact between drivers. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the operator had no lawful basis under Article 6(1), because other employees are not parties to the employment contract, and that the publication was not necessary under section 3 of the Finnish Act on Protection of Privacy in Working Life. The operator was given a reprimand and ordered to bring its processing into line with the GDPR by reassessing the publication of the numbers.

A parent complained to the Slovenian Information Commissioner that the organiser of a school competition had not given her access to her minor daughter's placement and award, which she had first requested on 19 December 2022. The organiser did not decide on the request within one month, and the Commissioner found that it infringed Article 15 GDPR read with Article 12 GDPR and Article 14 ZVOP-2 at the time of the complaint on 2 May 2023. The organiser later disclosed the information on 7 May 2024, so the Commissioner ordered no further measures and imposed no fine.

A former contractor complained that the defendant had not closed his professional email account after the collaboration ended, had read incoming mail, and had given unsatisfactory answers to his requests for access, restriction and erasure of his data. The Litigation Chamber dismissed the complaint on expediency grounds, not on the merits. It found the complaint was accessory to a wider commercial and legal dispute (payment, contract termination, copyright, threats) better handled by the courts, and that a full investigation would be disproportionate. The decision states that this dismissal does not mean that no violation occurred.

A complainant reported that a music event organiser required a copy of the guardian's ID card, plus personal data of the guardian and of minors, on parental authorisation forms, and that the privacy notice was outdated. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings for alleged breaches of Article 5(1)(c) (data minimisation) and Article 13 (information duty), with proposed fines of EUR 3,000 and EUR 2,000. The company paid EUR 3,000 after two cumulative 20% reductions, which ends the procedure under Article 85 LPACAP and waives administrative appeal. The company also reported that it had adopted measures to prevent recurrence.

A club member complained that the controller had not properly decided her request to erase her and her daughter's personal data, made on 8 and 18 February 2024. The controller replied on 19 February that the data was deleted, but later said the erasure was done on 7 March 2024 and that it had informed her on 21 March. The Slovenian Information Commissioner found that the controller infringed Article 17 GDPR, read with Article 12 GDPR and Article 14 ZVOP-2, by failing to decide the request in time. No corrective order was made because the breach had been remedied, and the complainant was given full access to the file.

A complaint was lodged with the Spanish DPA about a company organising concerts and festivals. The company required a photocopy of the ID card of the adult authorising a minor to attend, and its parental-consent forms gave outdated privacy information. The DPA opened a sanctioning procedure for alleged breaches of Art. 5(1)(c) and Art. 13 GDPR and proposed fines of EUR 3,000 and EUR 2,000. The company paid EUR 3,000 with both the 20% admission-of-responsibility reduction and the 20% voluntary-payment reduction, and the DPA terminated the procedure.

A public healthcare facility reported a ransomware attack of 10 February 2022 that encrypted its servers holding data of about 30,000 patients and over 1,100 staff, including health data. The Polish DPA found that the facility had not carried out a risk analysis, had not adequately tested its security measures, and had not notified the data subjects of the breach. It imposed a fine of PLN 40,000 and ordered the facility to notify the affected people within 30 days and to bring its security measures into line within 90 days after a risk analysis. The infringement of security was found to be negligent, while the failure to notify was a conscious decision.

A parent with legal standing for his child complained that a primary school had not answered his access request in time, so it was deemed refused by silence. The school later sent the documents with some personal data and the child's address redacted, and gave its reasons on 13 March 2024. The Commissioner found that the school violated Article 15 in conjunction with Article 12 when it failed to decide on the request in time. It found no violation of Article 15 in respect of the later decision of 13 March 2024, which it held was late but justified.

A data subject complained that BBVA asked the credit-information file ASNEF-EQUIFAX to register his debt, but the notice of inclusion was sent to an incomplete address, so he only learned of the listing when it blocked his credit applications. The AEPD opened a sanctioning procedure for breach of the accuracy principle in Article 5(1)(d) GDPR and initially proposed a fine of EUR 200,000. BBVA paid EUR 120,000 on 6 June 2024, using both the 20% reduction for admitting responsibility and the 20% reduction for voluntary payment, which ended the procedure. The order to prove rectification of the data sent to the credit file was included in the initiation agreement and is part of the resolution.

A complainant said that an ex-partner had sent them, by email, car insurance policy data and a DGT vehicle report that the insurer's systems had produced, which the ex-partner had accessed without authorisation. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings on presumed breaches of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR, with a proposed fine of EUR 200,000 (140,000 and 60,000). The company paid EUR 160,000 after taking a 20% reduction, which ends the proceedings. The company was ordered to notify the AEPD within three months of measures on access traceability, confidentiality and security.

An individual (controller) was fined €10,000 for unlawfully publishing the names, addresses, telephone numbers, data concerning health and images of ten data subject on Telegram and YouTube with the aim of encouraging others to make abusive phone calls.

The DPA dismissed a complaint against a newspaper, finding that it was publishing information in the public interest and was thus exempt under national law from certain GDPR provisions. It noted that the exemption applies where there is a close nexus between the personal data published and the public interest - including where special categories of data are involved.

The Hungarian authority (NAIH) decided a complaint by a politician against Mediaworks Hungary Zrt., the publisher of several online news sites. The publisher had run articles about the complainant's alleged unlawful house construction, using photos of the house and entries from a construction log. The authority found the processing lawful under the legitimate interest basis in Article 6(1)(f) and rejected the complainant's requests on that point. It found breaches of the information duties in Article 14(1)-(3) (construction log data) and Article 13(1)-(2) (photographs and drone images), and issued a reprimand with no fine.

A citizen asked the Ministry of the Interior and Health for access to the CPR system's security log, which showed which organisations had historically subscribed to data about him. The ministry refused, citing the Danish Data Protection Act's exemption for public interests and its resource burden. After the CJEU ruling in C-579/21 (22 June 2023) on access to logs, Datatilsynet held that the ministry could not refuse access on that stated basis under Article 15 GDPR. Datatilsynet expressed no criticism of the ministry (the decision is tagged "Ingen kritik"), because its own long-standing practice had been that there was no right of access to security logs, which this decision changed. It expected the ministry to handle any new request in line with the decision.

An employee of a car dealership complained about two workplace systems: a facial recognition time-attendance device and a workshop management software that logged each mechanic's work and pauses. After an inspection by the Guardia di Finanza, the Garante found that biometric processing of employees had no valid legal basis, was disproportionate, kept biometric data until employment ended, and relied on an inadequate privacy notice. The management software was also used without a valid legal basis or adequate information. The Garante fined the company EUR 120,000, banned the biometric processing, and ordered the company to bring the software processing into compliance within 90 days.

The Garante investigated Eni Plenitude after 108 reports and 7 complaints about unsolicited telemarketing calls made without consent or to numbers listed in the Public Opposition Register. It found breaches of the principles of lawfulness, fairness, accuracy and security, telemarketing without a valid legal basis, and failure to put in place security measures and monitoring over the whole sales chain. It imposed a fine of EUR 6,419,631 (2% of the maximum), a ban on further processing of the complainants' data, and orders to inform 657 data subjects and strengthen controls. The decision is also published.

A complaint said the Comune di Ustica had published documents on its online notice board (Albo pretorio) that exposed personal data. Two determinations were still online: one named people receiving payments for transport to the mainland for cancer, dialysis or life-saving therapy, with their tax codes and IBANs, and the other gave farmers' names, tax codes, birth data and payment amounts. The municipality had also not communicated its DPO's contact details to the Garante. The Garante found breaches of the health-data publication ban, data minimisation, the rules on publication and retention, and the DPO notification duty. It imposed a fine of EUR 500 and ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A woman complained that a car rental company refused her a rental voucher because she was on a 'black list'. The investigation showed that the company's parent bank queried the public SCIPAFI identity-fraud system on its behalf, without Ministry authorisation, and passed the result to the rental company through an internal watchlist. The Garante found the processing unlawful, and also found that the data processing agreement between the bank and the rental company did not make the bank a valid processor. It fined the bank EUR 1,000,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The operative part cites Articles 12(3) and 15, while the reasoning deals with Articles 5(1)(a) and 28.

A local health authority answered a prison administration's request to verify a disability certificate by sending a full copy of the medical commission report. The back of the sheet showed the complainant's medical history in clear, including HIV infection. The authority blamed an operator's material error during a COVID staffing shortage. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching data minimisation, integrity/confidentiality and security obligations, and Article 75 of the Italian Code. It imposed a fine of EUR 24,000 and ordered publication, with no corrective orders since the conduct had ceased.

A woman complained that a car rental company refused her a rental because she was on a 'black list'. The Garante found that the company had used a fraud watchlist from its parent bank. That list drew on the state SCIPAFI identity-theft database, and the Ministry had not yet authorised access on the company's behalf. The privacy notice was too generic about these checks, and the processor arrangement with the bank did not hold up. The Garante fined the company EUR 250,000 and ordered the decision published. It did not order the notice to be corrected because the company had already updated it. A separate decision against the bank was adopted the same day.

A data subject asked the controller, a media company, for access to their personal data. The controller refused to act on an email request unless the person returned a signed form in person at its premises, showed a photo ID, and gave their personal identity code. The deputy ombudsman found that this practice breached the data minimisation principle (Art. 5(1)(c)) and Art. 12(6), and was unreasonably burdensome, not a means of facilitating rights under Art. 12(2). The deputy ordered the controller to change its practice and to handle the request again, and to report the measures taken by 28 August 2024. No fine was imposed, and the decision is final.

A customer asked the company to erase his data and stopped receiving marketing, but the company kept sending promotional emails for months and never answered his erasure and objection requests, even after the complaint was filed. The Litigation Chamber found negligence, noting the company still had not replied by the hearing date. It imposed an administrative fine, starting from an EDPB-guideline-based amount of EUR 245,000 and reducing it by about 30% to EUR 172,431 because of the company's financial situation.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation in April 2024 into Corint Logistic SRL after a customer complained about commercial SMS messages received despite having exercised the right to erasure. The authority found the company ignored erasure/objection requests, could not prove consent for marketing SMS, and did not answer access and erasure requests sent by email. It imposed two fines of RON 4,976.3 (about EUR 1,000 each) and a warning, plus corrective measures on consent-based direct marketing and on handling data subject requests.
The DPA fined a controller €300 for using a video surveillance camera for home security which captured a neighbor’s patio.
The APD issued a reprimand against a controller for responding orally to an access request and for not providing the information regarding the processing due to its apparent obviousness.

Hundreds of Greeks abroad registered on the special overseas electoral rolls complained after receiving unsolicited political e-mails from an MEP on the e-mail addresses they had given to the Ministry of Interior's platform. The Authority investigated both the MEP and the Ministry. The decision is a single text with two separate parts. Against the MEP, it found breaches of Article 5(1)(a) with Articles 6(1) and 14 GDPR, fined her EUR 40,000 and ordered deletion of the data. For the Ministry of Interior, it found breaches of the security, confidentiality, data protection by design, breach notification and records-of-processing provisions. It fined the Ministry EUR 400,000 and ordered it to document and review its data protection policies and measures, set a timetable, run audits and train staff. A decision on a political party and another individual was postponed.

Hundreds of Greeks living abroad complained that an MEP sent them an unsolicited political e-mail at the personal address they had given to register on the special overseas electoral rolls through the Ministry of Interior platform. The Authority found that the MEP processed overseas voters' e-mail addresses without a valid legal basis and without informing them, breaching the principle of lawfulness, objectivity and transparency (Art. 5(1)(a)), Art. 6(1) and Art. 14 GDPR. It fined the MEP EUR 40,000 and ordered her to erase all the overseas voters' data. In the same decision it fined the Ministry of Interior EUR 400,000 for security and accountability failings, and it postponed the decision on a political party and another person.

A person who had reported a female professional for misusing the title 'architect' complained that the Matera architects' association disclosed the complainant's identity and contact details to the reported professional, and published council minutes naming the complainant in full. The minutes also wrongly attributed the report to an unrelated councillor with the same name. The Garante found breaches of the principles of lawfulness and accuracy, of Article 6 and of Article 2-ter of the Italian Code, and imposed fines totalling EUR 3,500 across two conducts. The late publication of the DPO contact details breached Article 37(7), for which the association received only a reprimand.

A patient asked the Rhodense health authority to correct his residence and health-domicile addresses, sending the request to its general institutional certified email. The authority did not answer for 156 days and corrected the data only after he complained to the Garante. The Garante held that the general institutional address was not a 'random or incorrect' address under the EDPB access guidelines, so the request had to be handled within the Article 12 deadlines. It found breaches of the accuracy principle and of Articles 12 and 16, and imposed a fine of EUR 4,500 plus publication of the decision. No corrective orders were needed because the conduct had ended.

A secretary of a neurology outpatient clinic of the local health authority ASL TO4 emailed a circular on therapeutic plans to 45 multiple sclerosis patients, with all addresses visible in the CC field, and then sent a correction the same way. This disclosed the patients' health status to each other. The authority notified the breach and the Garante found a violation of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR. It rejected the defence of excusable human error. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,400 and ordered publication of the decision, with no corrective orders since the conduct had ceased and measures were being implemented.

A tenant complained to the Belgian DPA about a dishwasher seller whose technician allegedly obtained the landlord's contact details and used them to send the landlord an invoice for damage caused during a home visit. The Litigation Chamber found that the complainant was not the data subject and had not shown any interest in acting on the landlord's behalf, so the complaint had no standing. It dismissed the complaint on technical grounds, without examining the merits, and noted that the matter appeared to be a side dispute to a wider liability dispute between the parties.

The Spanish DPA fined CUBILLO GALLEGO, S.L., a real estate company, EUR 3,000 for breaching Article 13 GDPR. A complainant said the website privacy policy did not properly identify the controller, gave a contact email that was not the company's real one, and omitted the retention period and the right to complain to a supervisory authority. The DPA found these gaps, and also found that a sales contract collected data without the required information. The company did not respond to the DPA's transfer request or the opening of proceedings, so the start agreement was treated as the proposal. The company was also ordered to correct its privacy policy and contracts within one month.

A complainant was dismissed with immediate effect after the municipal administration reviewed images from its outdoor video surveillance system to specify the serious misconduct alleged against her. The CNPD's restricted formation found that the cameras were authorised for security purposes only, so using the footage to justify the dismissal was an incompatible further processing in breach of Article 5(1)(b) GDPR. It issued a reprimand and did not impose an administrative fine, nor the compliance order or publication proposed by the investigating officer.

The Polish data protection authority found that a medical services company had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures. It had no proper risk analysis, outdated system software on edge devices, configuration errors and no procedures for regularly testing security measures. The case began with the company's own breach notification and an inspection. The authority ordered the company to fix its processing within 30 days and imposed an administrative fine of PLN 1,440,549, equal to EUR 330,000, using the EDPB Guidelines 04/2022 method.
The DPA held that the use of a data subject’s email address for political advertising purposes must be based on consent.

The Dutch DPA fined Clearview AI Inc., a US company offering facial recognition services built on billions of photos scraped from the internet, a total of EUR 30.5 million. It found unlawful processing of personal data and biometric data of people in the Netherlands, insufficient information to data subjects, failure to answer two access requests and failure to facilitate access rights. The missing EU representative (Art. 27) was also an infringement, but no fine was imposed for it because the Italian and Greek authorities had already fined it. The AP also imposed four periodic penalty payments to force Clearview to end the continuing infringements. Clearview refused to provide turnover information, so the AP used the EUR 20 million maximum as the basis.

The DPA issued a reprimand to the Birmingham Children’s Trust Community Interest Company for a data breach related to the production of a child care protection plan that included inappropriate personal data in the form of criminal allegations against a child.

The DPA considered that its intervention in a case regarding the installation of surveillance cameras in the common areas of a co-owned building was not strictly necessary, as it was an ancillary to a broader dispute. Therefore, the DPA dismissed the case.

The Romanian DPA published a press release covering two investigations, one against Medicover SRL and one against Iridex Group Salubrizare SRL. For Iridex, the investigation began after a complaint from an individual. The company sent a collective email to its clients in which all the email addresses were visible to every recipient. The authority found it had not ensured that people acting under its authority process data only on its instructions, and had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the company RON 9,951.80, stated as equivalent to EUR 2,000.

The Romanian data protection authority announced in a press release that it had finished two investigations and found breaches of Article 32 GDPR. Medicover SRL was fined RON 4,970.30 (stated as EUR 1,000) after it notified a personal data breach: a medical consultation report was handed to another patient who was not meant to receive it. The authority found that the controller had not ensured that people acting under its authority process data only on its instructions, and had not put in place technical and organisational measures giving security suited to the risk. The release also covers a second controller, a waste-management company, which is not part of this record.

A man complained that he received a promotional email from a hotel company he had never dealt with, and that his access request went unanswered. The company could not show consent or where it got his data, gave contradictory answers to the Garante, and deleted his data after the investigation began. The Garante found breaches of the consent rules for marketing and of the right of access, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the order.

A professional health technician complained that the provincial professional order of technical health workers in Mantua sent an email to him and about forty other professionals, asking for their employers' details, with all recipients' addresses visible in the 'To' field. The order said it was a purely material error. The Garante found that disclosing the recipients' email addresses and, indirectly, their unvaccinated status had no legal basis, in breach of Article 5(1)(a) and Article 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Italian Code, and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 plus publication of the decision.

A data subject complained that a sports club company had not answered his access request, sent on 20/07/2020, for his personal data and a copy of the privacy notice. The company gave no reply within the deadline and did not explain why. It also failed to answer the Authority's information requests, though the Authority dropped that separate charge because the requests had not been correctly delivered. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 3,000, and ordered the company to answer the request and to publish the decision.

The Garante examined four breach notifications and one complaint about improper access to patients' electronic health dossiers at the Padua university hospital. Health staff looked at records of patients they were no longer treating, to review outcomes of earlier cases. In other cases unknown persons used the credentials of staff who left workstations open, and an administrative employee accessed a patient-employee's dossier without any care purpose. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), (c), (f), 9, 25 and 32 GDPR. It imposed three fines of EUR 25,000 each (EUR 75,000 in total), ordered the hospital to remove two access reasons from the system, requested further information and ordered publication.
The document is an opinion of the Data Protection Authority on the draft regulation for digital infrastructure and cloud services for public administration.

An employee of the hospital emailed her department head to say she was ill and could not work her next shift, describing her symptoms so that a replacement could be found. The head of the unit replied and copied in the Director General, who was the hospital's legal representative and data controller. The Garante held that forwarding the full email, including health information, to the Director General was not necessary for managing the work and was unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 9 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Italian Code. It issued a reprimand and no fine, citing the single data subject, negligence, cooperation and no relevant prior violations.

The Italian Data Protection Authority held a meeting on May 9, 2024, involving key members, to address a significant data breach incident affecting the "Ordine degli Avvocati di Roma" and managed by InfoCert S.p.a.

An unauthorized third party requested and obtained a duplicate SIM card for the complainant's Lowi mobile line without proper identity verification by Vodafone. This SIM swapping allowed the third party to access the complainant's personal data and bank accounts, carrying out fraudulent financial transactions. The AEPD concluded that Vodafone failed to act with the required diligence to verify the applicant's identity, resulting in an unlawful processing of personal data under Article 6(1) GDPR. Consequently, the AEPD imposed an administrative fine of EUR 200,000 on Vodafone España, S.A.U.

The Romanian authority's press release reports two investigations opened after personal data breach notifications. For Centrul Medical Unirea SRL, personal data of many patients and employees were disclosed on the internet without authorisation. The authority found inadequate technical and organisational security measures and fined the company RON 24,856 (about EUR 5,000), also ordering a review and update of its measures. A second operator, Genpact România SRL, was fined separately, which is outside this record.

Datatilsynet issued serious criticism (alvorlig kritik) to the City of Copenhagen over a personal data breach. During a disk move in April 2021, a human error by an administrator gave about 37,500 administrative IT users access to a drive holding data on up to 3.7 million people, including children's school, wellbeing, language assessment, dental and health care information. The access lasted about two months until a routine network scan found it, and the municipality reported the breach. Datatilsynet found that the city had not ensured access was limited to staff with a work-related need, had a set-up where one error could expose 3.7 million people, and had not tested access rights right after the move. No fine was imposed.

4Finance Spain (VIVUS) notified the AEPD of a personal data breach in which attackers used valid customer credentials to log into customer web areas and take out fraudulent loans, affecting about 9,500 customers. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings for breach of Art. 5(1)(f) (proposed fine EUR 200,000) and Art. 32 GDPR (proposed fine EUR 400,000), a total of EUR 600,000. The company paid EUR 360,000 on 25 April 2024, applying both 20% reductions (acknowledging responsibility and voluntary payment). The AEPD therefore declared the proceedings terminated under Art. 85 LPACAP.

The DPA confirmed its previous fine of €70,000 on a bank, finding that it lacked a legal basis to process personal data that was stolen and that the controller was negligent in verifying the identity of the data subject for a credit application.

The complainant asked the respondent for access to his personal data on 7 February 2024 and repeated the request on 3 March 2024, asking in particular for the source of his data after receiving a magazine he said he had not subscribed to. He got no reply within one month. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision under Article 95 WOG. It stated that the respondent possibly infringed Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 15(1) GDPR and ordered it to comply with the access request under Article 58(2)(c) GDPR. The decision is not a decision on the merits and imposes no fine.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision (no. 71/2024, 6 May 2024) after a former executive complained that her company had kept her professional mailbox open after she left in September 2022, that automatic replies were still sent in January 2023, and that her access request was answered late. The Chamber found suspected infringements of Articles 5(1)(a), 6(1), 12(3), 13(1)(c) and 25 GDPR, but this was not a merits decision. It issued a warning for the lack of a sound policy on closing former employees' business mailboxes. The mailbox had been closed in the meantime, so no further corrective measures were ordered and no fine was imposed.

A data subject with special status complained that the controller had forged court documents by reissuing payment-reminder duplicates and an interest calculation that showed addresses he said he never lived at, and that it had not told him the source of those addresses. The Commissioner found that the reissued duplicates and the interest calculation carried inaccurate addresses, which breached the accuracy principle in Article 5(1)(d). It found no forgery and no breach of the right of access under Article 15(1)(g). No corrective order or fine was imposed, because the controller had already corrected the documents and changed its practice.

A data subject asked a mobile operator in July 2018 to delete all his data. The operator refused for data linked to a phone subscription cancelled in 2019, which it may keep for three years after the customer relationship ends. It found no basis to refuse for data linked to a customer relationship that ended in 2007, which should have been deleted automatically earlier; that data was deleted manually in March 2020. The Deputy Ombudsman issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b). This decision replaces the decision of 23.4.2024 with the same file number, which was corrected at the controller's request.

A bank customer complained that an employee of the bank had repeatedly consulted his personal data without a professional reason. The bank said it had taken necessary and proportionate measures against the employee and had notified the breach to the authority. The Litigation Chamber dismissed the complaint on opportunity grounds, without examining it on the merits. It reasoned that the subject of the complaint seemed resolved by the measures taken, and that the complaint was a side issue to a wider dispute (stalking) that belongs to the courts and the police.

The Dutch DPA (AP) looked at the cookie practices of kruidvat.nl, run by A.S. Watson, in a 2019 review of several websites, and in November 2019 wrote to the company that it probably did not comply with the rules; checks in 2020 showed it had not changed its practice. The AP found that tracking cookies were placed without valid consent between 28 April 2020 and 1 October 2020, so there was no lawful basis for the processing. It imposed a fine of EUR 600,000 under category III of its fining policy, taking the group's turnover into account and treating the long delay since the investigation report as mitigating. The company has lodged an objection (a request to the AP to reconsider) against the decision.

Following a ransomware attack involving data from the Federal Government, the Federal Data Protection and Transparency Officer reprimanded a software provider for its lack of appropriate measures to ensure data protection.

The DPA held that a municipality processing a third party’s criminal data to adequately justify a marriage refusal decision was disproportionate and could have been attained by less intrusive measures, for example anonymisation of the data.

A Polish sports association published a participant list on its social media page that contained more personal data than needed, including e-mail addresses and birth dates, affecting over 100 people. The association did not notify the UODO of the breach within 72 hours and did not respond fully to repeated requests for explanations. The UODO found a breach of Article 33(1) GDPR and imposed an administrative fine of PLN 916.71, stated as about EUR 210. The decision is marked final.
The DPA fined a company €54,600 after the loss of a flash drive containing unencrypted employee data led to a data breach.

The DPA fined a postal service €12,680 (HUF 5 million) for adding unsolicited content to its delivery updates. While a customer satisfaction questionnaire did not require a separate legal basis, the inclusion of direct marketing information did.

As part of the EDPB coordinated action on data protection officers, the Greek authority sent a questionnaire to 31 public bodies, including the Ministry of Climate Crisis and Civil Protection. The Ministry did not answer on time, even after a reminder, and had not designated a DPO or published or notified DPO contact details since its creation. It also had not complied with GDPR chapters 3 and 4 (transparency, data protection by design and default, records of processing, security). The Authority found violations of Articles 31, 37, 12, 32, 25, 30 and 5(1)(a), (c), (f), and imposed three fines totalling EUR 50,000. The Ministry's arguments about being newly created and lacking resources were rejected.

The DPA found that the administrator of a software platform allowing people to book doctor's appointments was a processor as it did not determine the purposes of the processing, and did therefore not have to respond to an access request. The purposes were determined by the health care institutions.

An entry in the CNIL's list of sanctions, dated 25 April 2024, concerns an association that takes part in the activities of political organisations. The CNIL dealt with it under its simplified procedure and fined it EUR 16,000, with an injunction, for lacking a legal basis. The list gives no reasoning, no articles and no facts of the case. A later entry of the same kind, dated 23 October 2024, records a penalty payment of EUR 4,000 for not answering an injunction; the list names nobody, so it does not say whether it is the same association.

The local police reported a shop run by Dly S.r.l. in a shopping centre, and the Guardia di finanza inspected it on 5 July 2023. It found six working cameras that filmed customers and employees, viewable live and recorded on the owners' private smartphones. The system was installed without a union agreement or Labour Inspectorate authorisation, as Article 4 of Law 300/1970 requires. An authorisation from 2019 for a different shop did not count. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned it until the safeguards are in place, and fined the company EUR 5,000.

The Garante received a referral from the Nuoro labour inspectorate after finding that an employee of a patronato (a private body providing assistance services, run by INPAS) kept working and handling user files after the patronato had notified the end of his employment to the employment centre, without a formal dismissal. The patronato had let him keep access to the platforms and to users' personal data, including special-category data, so he processed that data without a legal basis or authorisation. The Garante found the patronato had unlawfully disclosed personal data to a third party, in breach of Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 9 GDPR and Articles 2-ter and 2-sexies of the Codice, and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 plus an order to publish the decision on the Garante's website.

A temporary agency worker placed with the company complained that it did not give him copies of his training certificates after his access request. The company said it had deleted the certificates after the employment ended and did not state reasons for refusal or mention the right to complain. Only after the Garante opened the investigation did it obtain and send some certificates, almost eleven months later. The Garante found a breach of Article 12 in relation to Article 15 GDPR and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

A former employee of GSE complained that the company never answered his access requests of October and December 2021 for his performance evaluation files for 2019 and 2020. The company only supplied the documents in September 2022, about eleven months after the first request and after learning of the complaint to the Garante. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR, rejected the excuse of an IT mishap and the argument that the employee already knew the content. It fined the company EUR 30,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A complainant received unsolicited promotional emails from an e-commerce paper company, then dozens of anomalous emails, and got no reply to his rights request, which the company said ended up in spam. The Garante's technical checks showed the company's website ran an obsolete PrestaShop CMS with known serious vulnerabilities, even after the authority contacted it. It found violations of security and accountability duties, of data subject rights and of the lawful basis and consent rules for marketing. It ordered the company to update its security measures and pay a EUR 30,000 fine. The missing breach notification was treated as absorbed in the security violation.

A public employee complained that the Ministry of Justice's prison administration opened a disciplinary procedure against him after colleagues found his sex-work advert on a dating site and the prison management forwarded it, with images and details, to the central disciplinary office. The Garante found that collecting and further processing data on his sexual life and sexual orientation had no valid legal basis and breached national rules barring employers from acquiring information on the private life of employees. It found violations of Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 9 and 88 GDPR and issued a reprimand instead of a fine, citing the single data subject, the error, the closed disciplinary case, the security measures and the Ministry's cooperation.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation into Alpha Bank Romania SA after the bank notified a personal data breach. One of the bank's record systems had been wrongly administered by an employee, which led to unauthorised disclosure of and access to the data of a number of customers. The authority found that the bank had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures, nor sufficient steps to make sure persons acting under its authority process data only on its instructions. It imposed a contravention fine of 9,950.60 lei, equivalent to EUR 2,000.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in April 2024 into Tensa Art Design S.A., owner of the website lensa.ro. A complainant said the company used his phone number for direct marketing SMS messages without his consent. The company could not prove consent or any other legal basis, so the authority found a breach of Article 6 GDPR. It fined the company RON 9,941 (about EUR 2,000) and ordered it to ensure future processing complies, with no marketing processing without consent or another legal basis.

The complainant had to hand over his identity card as a deposit to rent equipment for visiting the respondent's domain, and got it back at the end of the day. He objected that this was not lawful, and the respondent said the practice was permitted if no copies were made, pointing to a EUR 100 alternative in its park rules. The Litigation Chamber held, on a prima facie basis, that the holding and retention of the identity card as a deposit may breach the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. It issued a warning under Article 58(2)(a) GDPR and Article 95 §1 4° of the Belgian DPA Act. It is not a merits decision, and the respondent may ask for reconsideration within 30 days.

Clyde Valley Housing Association have received a reprimand from the commissioner because of an infringement that occurred in July 2022 when they released a new customer portal with data subjects personal information visible to all other residents.

A complainant asked Google to delist search results linked to his name that reported his detention and investigation in a criminal case. Google refused for most of the links, citing the public role of the complainant and the public interest in the information. The Authority found the complainant is not a public figure, that the articles were old and no longer relevant, and that the privacy interest outweighed the public's right to information. It ordered Google LLC to delete the listed links from name-based search results and to confirm that other links with the same content do not appear, or delete them.

A patient complained that a receptionist at the clinic's diagnostic centre phoned her mobile number to give her test results to her father, without her consent and without identity checks. The clinic said the number was given by the patient herself at her visit, that no health information was disclosed on the call, and that it had since changed its procedures. The Authority found it could not establish what was said on the call, that the phone number was collected from the patient's own oral statement, and that the clinic complied with Articles 24(1)-(2) and 32 GDPR. It dismissed the complaint and did not use its corrective powers.

A customer complained that CaixaBank's form for updating customer data (Model 5433) contained a pre-set clause saying the customer consented to the bank requesting data from the Social Security Treasury for anti-money-laundering checks, with no option to refuse. The AEPD opened a sanction procedure for breach of Article 6(1) GDPR and proposed a fine of EUR 2,000,000. CaixaBank paid EUR 1,200,000 on 28 March 2024, using both the 20% reduction for admitting responsibility and the 20% reduction for voluntary payment. The Director therefore declared the procedure terminated under Article 85 of Law 39/2015. The bank also reported having changed its processes.

A complainant reported that an online grocery-shopping website collected personal and payment data without identifying the controller or giving the required privacy information. The Spanish authority found that the website did not identify the controller, DPO or the right to complain to the AEPD, which breaches Article 13 GDPR. The operator did not respond to the opening agreement, which was treated as a proposal of resolution. The authority imposed a fine of EUR 600 and ordered the website to publish a compliant privacy policy within one month.

The Rome Chamber of Commerce notified a personal data breach: an SQL injection attack on the CMS of its website let attackers reach a backup copy of the online appointment system database, which was then published online. About 22,300 users' identity, contact and login data were exposed. The Garante found that Innova Camera, the Chamber's processor, had kept the old backup far longer than needed and had stored passwords with the weak MD5 hash. It fined Innova Camera EUR 25,000 in total (EUR 10,000 for storage limitation and EUR 15,000 for integrity/confidentiality and security), and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because remedial measures had already been taken.

The Italian DPA checked the website of the Libero Consorzio comunale di Enna and found no DPO contact details and no notification of them to the Authority. The investigation showed the DPO was designated more than three and a half years after the GDPR applied, contact details were published and communicated late, and the DPO was an employee running several services, lacking time and exposed to conflicts of interest. The Garante found violations of Articles 37(1) and (7) and 38(2) and (6) GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 6,000, plus publication of the decision.

A municipal police inspection of a fruit shop found four operating video surveillance cameras with no information signs. The Garante found that the processing breached the transparency principle in Article 5(1)(a) and the information duty in Article 13 GDPR. The sole trader did not submit any defence. The Garante imposed a fine of EUR 1,000, ordered the trader to post information signs, and required a documented response within 90 days.

The Garante investigated an energy supplier after 56 reports and 2 complaints about unsolicited telemarketing calls that led to unrequested energy contract activations. A check with the Public Opposition Register showed 106 numbers in a sample week had been called while registered.
