The Garante found failures of accountability, lawful basis, security and control over the sales chain and partners, and breach of Art. 130 of the Code. It banned further processing of the complainants' data, ordered notification to the 106 people and better controls over the sales network, and fined the company EUR 100,000, also ordering publication.

The Garante investigated Olimpia S.r.l., an energy supplier, after 18 reports and 2 complaints about unwanted telemarketing calls. A check on a sample week showed that 34 telephone numbers registered in the Public Opposition Register had been contacted and later signed contracts. The Garante found breaches of lawfulness and accountability principles and of the consent rule, plus a lack of adequate controls over the sales chain and partners. The charges under Articles 5(1)(f), 25 and 32 were dropped. It imposed a fine of EUR 100,000, a ban on further processing of the complainants' data, orders to inform the 34 data subjects and to put controls in place, and publication of the decision.

A candidate in a public competition for 1858 social protection posts complained that INPS had published on its website lists of admitted and non-admitted candidates and the title evaluation with scores for each candidate. The Garante found that data of over 5,000 candidates were published and indexed by search engines without a suitable legal basis, since only final rankings of winners may be published, not intermediate results. It found breaches of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Article 2-ter of the Code, and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 plus publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered as the lists had already been removed.

A municipal employee reported that the municipality of Madignano had installed a video surveillance camera in its entrance hall near the attendance-recording clocks without a union agreement, and had used the footage in disciplinary charges against her. The Garante found the processing unlawful: the camera was used for employee monitoring and disciplinary purposes without meeting the labour-law conditions on remote monitoring, and without proper information to workers and visitors. It fined the municipality EUR 3,000, ordered it to give data subjects a proper privacy notice and report back within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

The President of the Czech Office dismissed the company's appeal against the first-instance decision of 14 March 2022. That decision found the company liable for two administrative offences under the Czech Personal Data Processing Act: passing pseudonymised browsing-related data of users of an antivirus program and its browser extensions to another controller for statistical trend analysis without a legal basis (Art. 6(1) GDPR), and failing to give the required information at collection (Art. 13(1) GDPR), both for at least two months in 2019. The appeal decision upheld the fine of CZK 351,000,000 and clarified the description of the data.

The Spanish DPA terminated sanctioning procedure PS/00483/2023 against Burgos Club de Fútbol, S.A.D. after the club acknowledged responsibility and paid 120,000 euros with two cumulative 20% reductions. The case concerned a fingerprint-based access system for the stand of the stadium, compulsory from 4 November 2022 and voluntary from 15 February 2023, for about 700 season ticket holders, including minors, without a prior DPIA or adequate information. The resolution confirmed the provisional suspension and, as a corrective measure, prohibited the fingerprint processing for stadium access.

The Federal Data Protection and Information Commissioner investigated an association that runs the 'Pfarrer-Check' campaign. It lists church staff by name in an online database with the status 'recorded' or 'asked', and it refused deletion requests from people whose details were already public elsewhere. The Commissioner opened an investigation in December 2023 and ruled in April 2024. The association may no longer list people with the status 'erfasst' (recorded) or 'angefragt' (asked) without valid prior consent. The deletion order is narrower: it covers only the entries of people whose data is already published elsewhere and who are recorded as 'erfasst' or 'angefragt', and these must be deleted within 40 days of the decision becoming final, unless those people give valid consent in that period. The association was charged CHF 3,750 in procedural fees. No fine was imposed; the decision only warns of a possible criminal fine under Art. 63 DSG for deliberate non-compliance.
The Hellenic DPA decided the deletion of the data subject from the List of Inadmissible Third Country Nationals based on a special provision of the immigration legislation.

The CNIL restricted committee fined the retail subsidiary (named X in the published text) EUR 525,000 for marketing failures. It bought prospect files from data brokers and sent SMS and made phone calls without valid consent, in breach of the French electronic marketing rule (L.34-5 CPCE) and Articles 6 and 14 GDPR. The committee also found that Article 32 GDPR was not breached. The decision is to be published for two years without naming the company after that.

The Greek DPA investigated, on its own initiative, the Ministry of Migration and Asylum's 'Centaur' (CCTV, drones and behavioural analytics) and 'Hyperion' (biometric entry/exit control) systems in migrant reception and closed-controlled facilities on the Aegean islands. It found that no complete, overall and coherent data protection impact assessment had been carried out by design and before the systems were procured and deployed (Articles 25 and 35 GDPR), and fined the Ministry EUR 100,000. It also found that the Ministry failed to cooperate with the Authority, giving unclear, incomplete and contradictory answers and withholding processor contracts (Article 31 GDPR), and fined it EUR 75,000. The total fine is EUR 175,000, and the Ministry was ordered to complete its compliance within three months.

The DPA found a controller rightfully declined an erasure request in accordance with Article 17(3)(e) GDPR since the controller demonstrated that the data is needed for future criminal proceedings against the data subject.
The DPA considered that the possibility that personal data could contribute as evidence in a legal action in the future justifies the refusal to comply with an erasure request.

A complainant asked an organisation (the decision calls it Y) for access under Article 15 GDPR after an employee at its embassy had, for private reasons, consulted her National Register data. The organisation answered more than three months after the request, well beyond the extended deadline. Its reply also did not explain whether the employee's identity had to be disclosed, so the access answer was incomplete. The Chambre Contentieuse issued a warning (an avertissement under Article 58(2)(a) GDPR) as a prima facie decision, not a decision on the merits, and gave the organisation 30 days to request a merits hearing.

The Latvian Data State Inspectorate (DVI) fined the publisher JK Media group SIA EUR 1,000. The company had not complied with an earlier DVI order of 10 January 2024 to edit or delete articles on its website that contained a complainant's name and photographs, and it had not answered the complainant's erasure request. The company said the links were removed in March 2024 after technical work on archived material. DVI found the breaches intentional and continuing, and it raised the provisional fine of EUR 332.01 to EUR 1,000.

The Slovenian Information Commissioner issued a misdemeanour decision against a legal person and its responsible director. Written debt-collection reminders sent to borrowers' employers contained identification, financial and economic personal data, and the decision finds that the security measures were inadequate and that no lawful basis existed for this disclosure. Both the responsible person and the legal person received a warning (reprimand) under the Slovenian data protection act (ZVOP-2), and no fine was imposed.

The DPA imposed a temporary ban on the Worldcoin Foundation's processing of biometric data, finding that it provided insufficient information for data subjects to consent, made it impossible to erase collected data or revoke consent, and collected large amounts of minors' sensitive data.

The DPA dismissed an appeal concerning an erasure request, finding that the controller made every necessary effort to delete images of the data subject from its social media, but was unable to delete all of the requested data as it awaited Meta's response.

The Catalan DPA fined FUOC €31,000 for violating Article 5(1)(c) GDPR by publishing a student’s project with excessive, non-anonymized data of 54 minors in its open-access repository, breaching the data minimisation principle.

A ransomware attack on the data centre run by LAZIOcrea, processor for the Lazio Region and several regional health bodies, made information systems of the local health authority Roma 3 unavailable, including systems holding patients' health data. The authority did not notify the breach to the Garante and did not document its reasoning or risk assessment for not notifying. The Garante found a violation of Article 33 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, rating the gravity as low. It took into account full cooperation, the Covid-19 emergency, late and partial information from the processor, and no previous infringements. The decision is to be published in full.

A ransomware attack hit the data centre run by LAZIOcrea, the in-house IT company of the Lazio Region, which was both controller for its own processing and processor for the Region, the Regional Council and several health service bodies. The Garante found that LAZIOcrea notified the breach late and incompletely as controller, informed the Region and the other controllers only about two weeks after the incident as processor, and had inadequate security measures in both roles. It set four separate fines (16,000, 25,000, 90,000 and 140,000 euro) totalling 271,000 euro and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because remedial measures had already been taken.

Following press reports from July 2023 about the Worldcoin project, the Garante opened an investigation into the Worldcoin Foundation. The project collects iris scans with the 'Orb' device to create a unique identifier, and links this to the WLD crypto-token, which is offered free in exchange for consent. The Garante found that the consent was probably not valid, because users lack sufficient information about the risks of biometric processing, the token incentive weakens consent, and there is no age check for users under 18. Rather than a fine, it issued a formal warning under Article 58(2)(a) GDPR that the processing, if carried out in Italy, would probably violate the GDPR, and ordered publication in the Official Gazette.

A data subject complained to the Slovenian Information Commissioner that a publisher had published an article disclosing his personal data, including his religious belief, without consent, and had not removed it after he asked for erasure. The Commissioner dismissed the complaint as not an administrative matter. Erasure requests made in the exercise of freedom of expression fall within the jurisdiction of the courts, not the supervisory authority. No special costs were incurred and the complaint was fee-free.
A residents association was fined €2,000 for posting a list of debtors in the building lobby and sharing it via email, in violation of the principle of confidentiality.

A complainant alleged that a bank (defendant 1) did not answer his access and erasure requests, and that a debt collection office (defendant 2) refused his erasure request and planned to keep his data for 10 years. The Litigation Chamber dismissed the complaint on grounds of opportunity, not on the merits. It found the complaint lacked the necessary evidence, that a thorough investigation would be disproportionate, and that the complaint was filed more than two years and nine months after the facts, so it was manifestly excessive under Article 57(4) GDPR. The decision does not find that a violation occurred.

The Norwegian DPA inspected NAV, the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration, on site in September 2023, focusing on access control, logging and log control in its case-handling IT systems. It found twelve deviations, one of which was dropped after NAV's reply, leaving eleven. It issued three compliance orders covering its governance system, access control and log control, with deadlines. It also imposed a combined administrative fine of NOK 20,000,000 for breaches of GDPR Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32, and of Article 5(2) and Article 24.

The Spanish DPA dismissed an internal appeal regarding a cookie banner decision, stating that the Spanish LSSI instead of the GDPR applies and that it would need to verify the data subject's claim which was not possible because the website was deactivated in the meanwhile.

A complainant objected to a bank (the decision calls it Y BANK) using his transaction data to build data models for personalised discounts on third-party products, arguing this was incompatible further processing that required consent. The Dispute Chamber found the model-building was a new purpose not compatible with the original payment purpose, but held that the bank could validly rely on legitimate interest under Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. It also found the bank met its transparency duties and gave timely effect to the objection, so the complaint was rejected.

An employee of a Subway restaurant complained that the store manager watched their work through CCTV and annotated screenshots with comments on their behaviour, and that staff were not informed about the monitoring. Persónuvernd found the monitoring was not for the declared security and property-protection purpose, amounted to monitoring of work performance without meeting the conditions, and that signage and information were inadequate. It fined Stjarnan ehf. ISK 1,500,000 and ordered deletion of the screenshots, correction of signage and information, and creation of a record of processing activities.

The DPA imposed a €330,000 (PLN 1,440,549) to a bank for failing to notify the DPA and data subjects of a data breach concerning banking documents which contained numerous personal data, including names and national identification numbers.
The DPA imposed a fine of €18,000 (PLN 78,575) on Toyota Bank for a failure to adequately assess the risk of a data breach and for not notifying the DPA as required by Article 33 GDPR.
The DPA found a hospital to have breached the principle of data minimisation by including unique and virtually permanent identification numbers in text messages sent to patients.

A complainant, through the Baden-Wurttemberg DPA, complained that Groupon required a copy of photographic ID before processing their access and erasure requests in 2018. The DPC found that the ID requirement breached data minimisation and that Groupon failed to comply with the initial access and erasure requests, and continued processing after the erasure request. The DPC found that Groupon had adequately shown the later erasure of the complainant's data, apart from limited administrative logs. The DPC issued a reprimand and imposed no administrative fine.

A complainant asked Apple to erase his Apple ID and email address in March 2019. Apple deactivated the account and kept a one-way hash of the email address, along with a DSID and transaction records, to prevent reuse of the address and to keep evidence of the deletion. The DPC ran an inquiry into the transparency of the information given to users and the legal bases for this retention. The decision, in its final part, finds infringements of Article 13(1)(c) and 13(1)(d) GDPR, issues Apple a reprimand, and orders Apple to revise its Apple ID Deletion Terms and Conditions. No administrative fine is imposed.

After a police inspection of a bar found two operating CCTV cameras inside the premises with no information signs and no authorisation under the workers' statute (art. 4 of Law 300/1970), the Garante declared the processing unlawful. The sole trader running the bar later said she had installed signs and obtained the labour inspectorate's authorisation, and sent photographs as proof. The Garante still found infringements of the transparency principle, the information duty and national rules on workplace monitoring, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A former bank employee complained that the bank gave only a partial reply to her access request for the data in her personnel file and in the disciplinary proceeding file. The bank sent the remaining documents (correspondence with a third party) only after the Garante intervened, and never told her why they had been withheld. The Garante rejected the bank's arguments, including that the access request served a different purpose, and found breaches of Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 15 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Two former employees (one a former chairman of the board) complained that the company kept their individual work email accounts active for months after they left and accessed the messages, and that it gave no proper information about this. The Garante found that the company kept the accounts active until 16 November 2021 and its legal representative accessed their content without a lawful basis, instead of deactivating them with an automatic reply. It also found the privacy notice did not cover this processing. The Garante found breaches of Article 5(1)(a), (c), (e) and Article 13 GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 20,000, ordered publication, and asked the company to report on an automatic account-deactivation system and Article 13 compliance within 90 days.

A complainant, acting as heir of her deceased father, asked the bank on 16 March 2023 for access to his personal data under Article 15 GDPR. The bank's replies were incomplete and late: it answered only after the Garante's office asked it to comment on the complaint, first in part in September 2023 and then in full on 2 October 2023. The Garante found that the bank failed to reply within the one-month deadline under Article 12(3) and failed to inform the complainant of the reasons for the delay and of her right to complain, as required by Article 12(4). It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 and ordered its publication, but did not order further corrective measures.
The DPA decided that both responsible person of a legal entity and the legal entity are held liable for processing of personal data of former employees without their consent.

After a complaint from a person who did not want to register to buy by card online, the Data Protection Ombudsman found that Verkkokauppa.com Oyj had required customer account creation for online purchases and had not set any retention period for customer account data. The Ombudsman found breaches of Article 5(1)(e) and Article 25(2) GDPR, ordered the company to set an appropriate retention period and change its registration requirement, and reprimanded it. The Sanctions Board of the Ombudsman's Office then fined the company EUR 856,000 for not setting a retention period; the registration requirement was not referred to the Board.

The UK Information Commissioner issued a monetary penalty notice against the Central YMCA, a charity running a Positive Health Programme for people living with HIV. On 6 October 2022 a co-ordinator sent an invitation email to a 270-recipient mailing list using the copy-to field rather than blind copy, exposing the addresses; a recall attempt caused a second email to all recipients. The Commissioner found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) and (2) UK GDPR, concerning appropriate security of special category data, and imposed a fine of £7,500 after a £300,000 starting figure under the ICO's five-step method was reduced. The Central YMCA accepted the Notice of Intent and the findings instead of making representations.

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation in February 2024 into a self-storage company that had notified a personal data breach after a cyber attack. The attack compromised the confidentiality and availability of customer data on its server, and the business was down for several weeks. The authority found that the company had not put appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place. It fined the company RON 24,884.50 (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to implement access monitoring and logging with at least 30 days of log retention, backed up.
The DPA reprimanded a controller for sending direct marketing offers without an option to opt-out while claiming during the investigation, that the processing in question was suspended.
